cells: DATA COLLECTION GUIDE  |  Tailor by Statistics, Modelling or Theoretical/Other
LIMITATIONS THAT MATTER MATHEMATICALLY  |  Compare methods → justify choice → identify effects on accuracy, bias, assumptions, validity or conclusions → mitigate or narrow the claim.

Data Collection guidance: identify SAMPLING, SOURCE, MEASUREMENT and INPUT limitations only. Do not show PMCC, regression, optimisation or other technique-specific weaknesses until that mathematics is being used in C40–C50.

Stage gate before matching: C20–C26 shows collection/source limitations only; C30 uses confirmed data notes but does not propose maths-technique weaknesses; C40–C50 can offer technique-specific examples. C60 revisits CONFIRMED limitations, no new catalogue.

Useful: 'A 0.1 s timing resolution and human reaction-time variation limit defensible precision in calculated speeds.' Not useful alone: 'The stopwatch was difficult to operate.' Do not invent error sizes.

If a limitation seriously undermines the intended inference, revise the method, aim or population instead of calling it acceptable. Define data-collection jargon and meaningful symbols only where needed.
Quality check and impact on interpretation
Who or what is your intended population, and what is one observation?
Short description: target population, unit, scope
Target population ≠ the convenient people you can reach; distinguish sampling frame.
State which population the conclusions can reasonably apply to.
When population is countable and potentially accessible
Could you include everyone (a census), rather than take a sample? What would that involve?
A census may make sense for a small school club; it need not be appropriate for all school students.
Judge the scope of the inference: census coverage, nonresponse and target-population mismatch matter mathematically; collection time by itself is a feasibility issue.
Which feasible methods could you use: simple random, stratified, systematic, cluster, opportunity/convenience or another?
Choose several to compare; optional Other
Show short definitions only when unfamiliar; don't overwhelm with method names.
Compare representativeness, coverage and potential bias for these methods; cost or convenience matters only if it changes what can reasonably be inferred.
How will people/observations actually be selected?
If claiming random selection, describe an implementable random procedure; avoid saying 'random' when volunteers opt in.
Explain how the chosen procedure affects selection bias and reproducibility.
If using a sample or census
Why is your sample size or accessible population adequate for what you want to compare?
More data can help, but size alone doesn't eliminate bias. Consider balanced groups and what is achievable.
Discuss effect of sample size on stability of estimates and comparisons, and distinguish small samples from selection bias. Do not make blanket claims about adequate size.
Who might not respond, and what kind of bias could this introduce?
Volunteer responses and nonresponse may systematically differ from those who did not answer.
Explain how you'll reduce bias, or limit the conclusions to the respondents.
Are questions neutral, clear and measurable? Have you tested them with a small pilot?
Short pilot check; examples when requested
Define what rating scales represent; don't treat '5/5 happiness' as a physical measurement to arbitrary precision.
Prioritise response bias, the validity of scales and what may be inferred from scores; piloting matters when it improves measurement validity, not as a logistical story.
Two numerical quantities measured per subject
Are the measurements paired correctly, using the same observation and compatible units?
Record height and reaction time for each person as a pair, not unmatched lists.
Assess measurement repeatability and whether potential confounding variables matter.
How were groups defined, and are measurement conditions reasonably comparable?
Different times, tools or ages may affect results as well as the factor being compared.
Justify fair comparison and explain important confounders/unequal group sizes.
How was the original dataset sampled or measured, who produced it, and which population does it represent?
You can choose a dataset, not retroactively choose its original sampling design.
Evaluate fit for the aim and cite sampling/method limitations honestly.
If data have missing values, filtering or outliers
What will you include/exclude, and how could that choice change your conclusions?
Don't discard inconvenient observations just to create the predicted correlation.
Justify filtering, record missing data and test sensitivity where feasible.
If data change with location, date or season
Could the timing/location of collection distort the apparent pattern?
A lunchtime survey might not describe morning behaviour; one season may not represent the year.
Justify scope and when it is reasonable to generalise.
Is your model based on collected measurements, existing published values, theoretical assumptions or a combination?
Not every model needs a statistical sample. A theoretical optimisation may need dimensions and constraints instead.
Only ask collection/sampling questions that apply to actual sources.
When model has inputs or parameters
Which inputs, parameters, constraints and units does your model need, and where will they come from?
For a storage-box model: L, w, h and volume V; note dimensions and constraints.
Justify how each important value relates to the real situation and intended use.
What feasible ways could you measure or estimate these inputs? Why prefer your chosen tool/source?

Compare phone-video timing and a handheld stopwatch in terms of time resolution, reaction-time variation, repeatability and possible systematic bias; equipment inconvenience alone is not a mathematical limitation.
Explain how the method affects estimated parameters, numerical accuracy and model fit. Mention practical effort only briefly when it changes the quality or amount of evidence.
When repeated empirical readings are feasible
Can readings be repeated, conditions controlled or instruments checked?
Repeat measurements can reveal variation, but repeated readings do not fix a systematic error.
Explain the likely dominant error and what can be controlled.
Which assumptions make the model manageable, and are they acceptable for its intended purpose?
Ignoring air resistance might work for a short low-speed example, but not all trajectories.
Explain which assumptions affect the mathematical validity of the model and over what range. A convenient simplification is acceptable only if the consequence for results is limited and justified.
Using estimated or published model parameters
Are the units, definitions, coverage and original measurement context of each source suitable?
Published constants/measurements may apply only within particular environments or scales.
Attribute sources; explain context differences and uncertainty where known.
For models that can be tested against observations
How will you check the model on real observations, ideally not exactly those used to fit its parameters?
A separate test or held-out observations is helpful when there are enough data, but isn't mandatory in every IA.
Distinguish a model fitting its original data from an independent check; a lack of validation limits confidence in model predictions, not just project logistics.
If deciding between different model forms
What other model could plausibly describe the situation, and how might you choose?
Linear vs exponential growth; compare context and residual behaviour rather than expected trend alone.
Justify a sensible fit and interpretable parameters.
If model is useful only over a limited domain
What range of input values/conditions is your model intended for?
An empirical model may not justify extrapolation far beyond measured inputs.
Outside the observed/input range, conclusions may be extrapolations that the mathematics cannot justify; restrict the domain or explicitly qualify the result.
When parameters are estimated or measurements uncertain
If a key measurement/parameter changes slightly, how much does the result change?
Small changes in measured radius may affect calculated volume noticeably.
Use reasonable sensitivity/uncertainty rather than fabricated precision.
If a modelling investigation also uses survey/sample observations
Are the input observations sampled? Would a census or a different sampling method improve the model's relevance?
Fitting a model to sampled data requires understanding sample bias and scope.
Avoid treating modelling and statistics as mutually exclusive.
If model has little/no collected data
What simple theoretical case or constraint demonstrates that the model is worth investigating?
For constrained optimisation, a diagram with correctly named lengths can be more useful than arbitrary collected data.
Explain assumptions without inventing a dataset or a sampling plan.
What mathematical object, claim, condition or simplified case are you investigating?
No requirement for a population or sampling procedure.
Give a meaningful definition and explain why the approach is suitable.
If applying ideas to a special context
Which assumptions, specialist terms, restrictions and notational choices must the reader understand?
Define the mathematical object precisely; introduce deeper techniques at first use.
State which conclusions follow from the assumptions or special cases. The fact that a proof/problem was time-consuming is not a mathematical limitation.
Unusual method or different course route
What aspect would you like to confirm with your teacher before relying on this method?
Keep the teacher-check-in branch and summary available.
Do not mark the mathematical approach as approved automatically.
What TWO or more plausible approaches could have produced useful evidence?
Only compare realistic choices the student could genuinely carry out; include sample/census or available datasets.
Evaluate methods primarily by their mathematical consequences: quality of measurements, representativeness, bias, assumptions and validity of conclusions.
Which approach did you actually choose, and WHY is it preferable for your investigation?
'It was easier' is not a sufficient mathematical justification. Explain why the chosen method produces evidence suitable for the aim, with acceptable error and inferential scope.
Practical feasibility may explain the selection of a method, but the discussion of limitations must focus on how the choice affects numerical results or conclusions.
Which limitation most affects the accuracy, validity or interpretation of your mathematics? What result or conclusion might it change?

Optional examples here come ONLY from Limitation Examples rows tagged C20-C26, and only for methods/measurements the student actually used. Ignore selected future techniques such as PMCC, regression and optimisation.

Student checks: Did our sampling/source/measurement affect quality, precision or representativeness? If so, what is the consequence for what can later be concluded? Save confirmed limitations, not a borrowed paragraph.
How have you reduced this mathematical limitation, or checked how strongly it affects the result?

Collection-stage checks: inspect sampling coverage, response/missingness, source metadata, repeat-measurement variability or instrument resolution. Residuals, PMCC outliers, goodness-of-fit and optimisation constraints are for later mathematics.

Do NOT offer technique-specific checks while collecting data, even when a technique was selected during Planning. Route those examples to mathematical exploration once the student uses the relevant maths.
Why is the remaining limitation acceptable for your investigation's aim, and exactly what does it stop you concluding?
E.g., an opportunity sample may support a cautious description of the participating club but not a claim about all teenagers; a model may be defensible only inside its measured range.
Do not automatically declare limitations acceptable. If they invalidate the aim, revisit the data or method or narrow the investigation focus; avoid outdated 'research question' template language.
When quantitative inputs or sourced rounded values exist
What instrument/source resolution and uncertainty can you actually justify?
A timer reading to 0.1 s does not prove ±0.1 s accuracy; separate instrument resolution, repeat variability and bias.
Name evidence for recording precision rather than inventing uncertainty values.
When making calculations/graphs from measured data
How many digits or decimal places should your results reasonably report, given the accuracy of the input data?
Retain guard digits for computation; round final reported values sensibly and apply consistently across tables, graphs and conclusions.
Measurement limitations affect defensible reporting; propagation may depend on the calculation.
If categorical, ranking or subjective ratings
Are these really numerical measurements, or categories/ordered responses?
A 1–5 agreement scale is not a physical quantity measured to 0.01 units.
Avoid spurious precision or invalid averaging/inference assumptions.
What symbol, meaning and units will you use for each important quantity?
Prefer h for height, t for time, L for length rather than x or y by default; conventional x/y are acceptable if clearly defined and helpful.
Use the symbols consistently in first graph and subsequent maths.
Would a reader outside the field understand this term without a brief explanation?
Define 'resting heart rate' or 'peak-hour traffic' before using measurements dependent on the definition.
Avoid a lengthy upfront dictionary; define at point of first use.
When a new mathematical technique appears later
Have you defined any new mathematical term or symbol just before it is introduced?
If a new parameter is introduced in a later regression step, define it there, not in the introduction.
This rule carries beyond data collection and should not be a compulsory initial glossary.
If data involve people, third-party sources or facilities
Do you have required permission/consent, and can a reader trace the source or procedure without identifying participants?
Link public dataset; anonymise participant-level data; respect unresolved permissions.
Teacher flag cannot be cleared by uploading a saved plan; no affected collection before approval.
If cleaning, calculating or discarding values
Which entries were missing, corrected, rounded, combined or excluded, and why?
Do not change values to make a pattern cleaner; keep an original record when possible.
A reader should understand any decision affecting the result.
What summary or initial graph would show what you collected without dumping all raw data into the IA?
Present only relevant short summaries in the main body. A traceable source is preferred; school guidance allows justified appendix data, although Pathfinder discourages long tables.
Use labels, units and chosen symbols; match displayed precision to measurement reality.
Why does this method generate evidence capable of answering your aim for the person who might benefit?
Ask what decision the evidence might reasonably inform, not 'what maths can I do with it?'
A limitation is useful here only if it affects whether the evidence supports an answer or advice. If serious, revise the question or method rather than justify unsupported conclusions.
If data are not yet collected

If your data have not arrived, which safe useful step could you do NOW: write the introduction, record a tentative prediction and WHY, define variables, compare methods, or check possible secondary sources?
Choose ONE now / I'm stuck → C95D / Source search → C95A / Save
Use the planned aim, motivation, beneficiary, data route and source choices. Candidate sources need checks of population, definitions, units, accuracy, provenance and permission before actual use.
Do not require data to work on the introduction/prediction, and don't imply a provisional model, planned graph or hypothetical dataset is evidence. Persist Pending status and return later.
CONTEXTUAL EXAMPLES  |  Show only if the student asks for help; never hand them an entire paragraph to copy.
I considered a census of all 24 members of our club instead of selecting a few volunteers.
A census could reduce selection bias within the club if most members respond; using only volunteers may systematically overrepresent engaged members.
This supports cautious statements about the club, not about the entire year group; nonresponse still matters.
The main limitation is possible bias in the estimates, not how long it took to collect answers.
My data came only from volunteers who responded to our club survey.
Selection bias could distort the estimated proportions or correlations, so I cannot automatically generalise to students who did not volunteer.
The sample might still allow a useful exploratory analysis of respondents; wider advice would require better coverage or a narrower aim.
'Responses were difficult to get' is not an evaluation unless it explains an effect on bias, sample size or inference.
I compared timing motion manually with estimating time from video frames.
Hand timing can introduce reaction-time variation; video timing has frame-rate and viewing constraints that can affect parameter estimates.
For a rough trend the resulting precision may be enough, but a precise acceleration estimate may need better evidence or uncertainty analysis.
The equipment being awkward is not itself mathematical; explain any effect on the data.
Time was recorded to the nearest 0.1 s, so displaying model predictions to six decimal places would suggest unwarranted precision.
Retain full precision while calculating, then justify the reported accuracy from measurements and model sensitivity.
Recorded resolution is not itself proof of true accuracy.
Cite a verified actual instrument or data-source resolution.
I use h for height (m), t for time (s) and v for speed (m/s).
Define symbols once where they first appear, then remain consistent in tables, equations and graphs.
New mathematical terms may be defined later just before they are needed.
Don't auto-assign x and y for every IA.
My investigation studies a geometrical constraint without taking measurements from a population.
Describe mathematical objects, assumptions and a simple case instead of inventing a census.
Teacher consultation still available for unusual scope.
Do not call theoretical examples a sampled dataset.

REFERENCE / SCOPE  ·  JIS SL Maths IA Guide (2025), especially slides 21–23 (method alternatives, limitations and sampling) and 27–28 (notation, definitions and numerical accuracy): https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1BesCf9vTKGLm588jx5SUIdLyz-x5HUyYb2LqG_BACKg/edit
These prompts support clear justification, reflection and communication; no particular data-collection technique guarantees marks. The student describes their own genuine decisions and evidence.
